Baháʼu'lláh, born Mirza Husayn-Ali in eighteen seventeen to eighteen ninety-two, was the founder of the Baháʼí Faith, a modern religion emphasizing the unity of humanity, religious pluralism, and world peace. Emerging from nineteenth-century Persia amid religious upheaval, he taught that all major religions are divine revelations addressing different stages of human development. Baháʼu'lláh was born into Persian nobility and initially became a follower of the Báb, a religious reformer whose execution profoundly shaped his spiritual mission. He is believed by Baháʼís to be a Manifestation of God, a figure through whom God reveals divine will to humanity, standing in a line with Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad. He spent most of his life imprisoned or exiled by Persian and Ottoman authorities for his religious teachings, enduring severe suffering that his followers view as redemptive. His core teachings emphasize the oneness of God, the oneness of religion, viewing all major faiths as expressions of eternal truth, and the oneness of humanity. The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, the Most Holy Book, is Baháʼu'lláh's primary written revelation, containing laws, practices, and spiritual guidance for the Baháʼí community. He established the Covenant, a spiritual and administrative framework ensuring unity and continuity in the faith after his death through designated successors. The Baháʼí Faith teaches progressive revelation, the idea that God continues to guide humanity through successive messengers as civilization develops and matures. His teachings addressed social issues including the elimination of prejudice, establishment of universal education, gender equality, and international peace—themes ahead of his era.
